title: The Machine Nobody Wanted
subtitle: Two Roland failures that rebuilt popular music

intro.age7: Two machines nobody wanted to buy changed music forever.
intro.age13: Roland made a drum machine and a bass machine that both failed. Because they failed they got cheap, and because they got cheap the right people got hold of them.
intro.adult: The economic chain from commercial failure to affordability to genre formation, told through the 808 and the 303.

framing.age13: Start with a drum machine that failed. The 808 did not sound like a drum kit, so it sold badly and was dropped after about three years. Press play and hear what people did not want.
framing.adult: The first failure: an instrument judged on realism, discontinued after roughly three years, and left to the secondhand market.

framing.age13: On 'Planet Rock' in 1982, the 808's machine sound is not a problem to hide. It is the point.
framing.adult: The reframing: the quality that sank the machine in shops becomes the reason to use it.

framing.age13: Roland's second failure was sold as a fake bass player. It was hard to program and did not sound like a bass guitar. Turn its knobs while it plays, which is exactly what nobody at Roland expected.
framing.adult: The pattern repeats with the 303: a product that missed its market, a cheap secondhand supply, and a use nobody designed for.

framing.age13: In Chicago, Phuture got a secondhand 303 without its manual and turned the knobs while it played. A whole genre is named after the sound that came out.
framing.adult: Access by people with no stake in the intended use: the step the whole thread has been building toward.

outro.age7: Being bad at the job you were built for is sometimes the best thing that can happen.
outro.age13: Neither machine was used the way it was designed. That is the pattern to watch for everywhere else on this map.
outro.adult: Sets up the machine-as-protagonist reading that recurs through the sampler, the four-track, and the dub plate.
